questions.question: When should a Java developer choose Azure Service Bus over Azure Event Hubs for messaging?
questions.title: Azure Service Bus vs Event Hubs — Messaging Choice for Java
questions.direct_answer: Use Service Bus for enterprise messaging patterns (queues, topics, dead-letter, sessions, at-most-once/at-least-once delivery). Use Event Hubs for high-throughput event streaming where you need replay and consumer groups — analogous to Kafka.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of messaging semantics — queues vs. streams, delivery guarantees, and when each model fits.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing Event Hubs for all messaging because it sounds more modern, missing that it lacks dead-letter queues and per-message TTL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Event Hubs Kafka surface — you can point a Kafka producer/consumer at Event Hubs without code changes.

sections.title: Does the Consumer Destroy the Message or Observe the Event?
sections.content:
The decision between Service Bus and Event Hubs comes down to one question: **does the consumer destroy the message, or does it observe the event?** Service Bus is a message broker — once a consumer acknowledges a message, it's gone from the queue. Event Hubs is a partitioned event log — consumers read events at their own offset, and the events remain in the log for days. These are fundamentally different messaging models, and picking the wrong one creates architectural problems that are expensive to fix later.

Service Bus supports enterprise messaging patterns that Event Hubs deliberately omits: dead-letter queues for failed messages, per-message TTL, duplicate detection windows, and sessions for ordered processing by partition key. When a payment processing pipeline needs to guarantee that a failed charge is inspected by an operator rather than silently dropped, Service Bus's dead-letter queue is the mechanism. Event Hubs has no equivalent — failed events require application-level error handling and a separate error topic.

The common mistake is choosing Event Hubs for all messaging because it handles higher throughput and sounds more modern. A payment command queue processing 50 messages per second needs Service Bus's delivery guarantees far more than it needs Event Hubs' million-event-per-second capacity. Conversely, a clickstream ingestion pipeline feeding analytics, audit, and ML consumers simultaneously needs Event Hubs' fan-out model — Service Bus subscriptions can't replay consumed messages.

sections.title: Broker vs Log — Where the Semantics Diverge
sections.content:
The table below highlights the capabilities that drive architectural decisions. These aren't feature checkboxes — each missing capability in Event Hubs forces you to build an alternative in application code.

| Capability | Azure Service Bus | Azure Event Hubs |
|---|---|---|
| Core model | Message broker (queue / pub-sub) | Partitioned event log (stream) |
| After consumption | Message deleted from queue | Event retained for configured window |
| Throughput | Thousands of operations/sec | Millions of events/sec |
| Dead-letter queue | Built-in, automatic on failure | Not available |
| Message replay | Not possible (consumed once) | Replay from any offset in retention |
| Per-message TTL | Configurable per message | Retention is partition-level only |
| Duplicate detection | Built-in time window | Not built-in |
| Ordered processing | Sessions (FIFO per session key) | Per-partition ordering only |
| Consumer model | Competing consumers (one wins) | Consumer groups (all read independently) |
| Kafka compatibility | Not available | Kafka wire protocol supported |
| Spring starter | `spring-cloud-azure-starter-servicebus` | `spring-cloud-azure-starter-eventhubs` |

sections.title: Command-Style Work vs Observation-Style Streaming
sections.content:
**Service Bus fits command-style messaging.** When a message represents work that must be processed exactly once — place an order, charge a card, send a notification — Service Bus guarantees that one consumer handles it. If processing fails after the maximum delivery count, the message moves to the dead-letter queue rather than being lost. Sessions enforce ordered processing per partition key, so all messages for `order-123` are processed sequentially even with multiple competing consumers.

The Spring integration uses `@ServiceBusListener` with automatic message completion on success and dead-letter on repeated failure. Your handler method focuses on business logic; the framework handles acknowledgment.

**Event Hubs fits observation-style streaming.** When multiple independent systems need to react to the same event — an analytics pipeline, an audit log, and a recommendation engine all observing user activity — Event Hubs lets each consumer group read the entire stream at its own pace. Replay is built in: if the analytics pipeline had a bug last Tuesday, you can reprocess from that offset without republishing events.

The **Kafka-compatible endpoint** is Event Hubs' underrated feature. You configure a standard Kafka producer with the Event Hubs namespace as the bootstrap server, and your existing Kafka client code works without modification. Authentication uses SASL/PLAIN with the Event Hubs connection string. This is a practical migration path for teams moving from self-managed Kafka to Azure without rewriting producer and consumer code.

sections.title: What Event Hubs Doesn't Have Will Surprise You
sections.content:
**Event Hubs lacks enterprise messaging primitives** that many developers assume are standard. There is no dead-letter queue — if your consumer throws an exception, you must handle the failure in application code by retrying, logging, or forwarding to an error topic. There is no per-message TTL — retention applies to the entire partition, not individual events. There is no built-in duplicate detection — idempotent processing is your responsibility.

Teams that choose Event Hubs for command-style workloads end up rebuilding these features in application code: a custom dead-letter topic, manual deduplication with a seen-ID cache, and TTL checks in the consumer. That's significant engineering effort to recreate what Service Bus provides out of the box.

The architecture that works best in practice often uses both services together. Event Hubs ingests high-volume events — clickstreams, telemetry, audit logs. A stream processor (Azure Stream Analytics or a Spring Cloud Stream consumer) enriches and filters those events, then publishes the resulting commands to Service Bus for reliable downstream processing. This gives you the throughput and fan-out of Event Hubs for observation, combined with the delivery guarantees of Service Bus for action.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Service Bus: each message delivered to one consumer; Event Hub: each consumer group reads the full stream** — Service Bus for transactional point-to-point or topic fan-out; Event Hub for parallel consumption of the same event stream by independent consumers
- **Service Bus dead-letter queue captures unprocessable messages** — messages that fail processing N times (or exceed TTL) move to the DLQ; inspect and replay from the DLQ without affecting the main queue
- **Event Hub retains events for replay** — default 1-7 days; consumers control their own offset; a new consumer group can replay from the beginning; Service Bus messages are deleted after `complete()`
- **Event Hub supports Kafka protocol** — `bootstrap.servers` points to the Event Hub namespace; existing Kafka clients connect without code changes; managed Kafka without cluster operations
- **Service Bus sessions for ordered per-entity processing** — a session ID groups related messages; a single consumer processes all messages for one session in order; essential for order state machines and workflow orchestration

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Service Bus and Event Hub both move messages between services, but they serve fundamentally different consumption models — Service Bus is a message broker for transactional workloads; Event Hub is an event stream for high-throughput ingestion.

**Service Bus — transactional message broker**
- Service Bus delivers a message to exactly one consumer from a queue — when the consumer reads a message and calls `complete()`, it's removed; if the consumer fails and calls `abandon()` or the lock expires, it becomes visible again for reprocessing
- Topics and subscriptions extend this with fan-out: one message published to a topic can be delivered to multiple subscriptions, each with its own filter and dead-letter queue
- Service Bus supports message sessions (ordered processing per entity), deferred messages, scheduled delivery, and dead-letter queues for unprocessable messages — which makes it the right choice for order processing, payment workflows, and any use case where each message must be processed exactly once with retry

**Event Hub — high-throughput event stream**
- Event Hub stores events in partitioned ordered logs — multiple consumer groups can independently read the same stream from different offsets, which means one stream of telemetry events can be consumed independently by a metrics aggregator, a real-time dashboard, and a cold storage archiver
- Events are retained for a configurable period (1-7 days by default, up to 90 days with Event Hub Premium) — which means consumers can replay events without the producer knowing or caring
- Event Hub supports Kafka protocol — existing Kafka producers and consumers can connect to Event Hub with only a connection string change, which makes it a managed Kafka alternative on Azure

**Spring integration**
- Spring Cloud Azure provides `spring-cloud-azure-starter-servicebus` with `ServiceBusSenderClient` and listener annotations; `spring-cloud-azure-starter-eventhubs` wraps Event Hub with reactive and batch consumers
